explanations.explanation: Right where the text puts it. Joseph collects all the money in Egypt and Canaan, and "he brought it into Pharaoh's palace" (Genesis 47:14). Joseph, Jacob's son, isn't pocketing a coin of it. That's a LOT of money going through one door, friend.

Potiphar, the Egyptian officer Joseph once served (Genesis 39:1), is a name from way back in Joseph's story, so I see why it popped up. But this money doesn't go to his house. Genesis 47:14 says Joseph brought it into Pharaoh's palace. Pharaoh is the king, so the king's palace is where it lands.

Storehouses are where the grain sits, so it's a fair guess. But the grain is what the people are buying. The money goes somewhere else. Genesis 47:14 says Joseph "brought it into Pharaoh's palace." Grain in the storehouses, money in the palace.

I'd love for this one to be true, friend, but it's not. The Egyptians' money is gone, and Joseph says, "Since the money is gone, I will sell you food in exchange for your livestock." (Genesis 47:16) He's still selling, just taking something different. Free food never comes up in this passage.

Right, it's false. Joseph says, "Then bring me your livestock… I will sell you food in exchange for your livestock." (Genesis 47:16) The money ran out, but the selling didn't stop. The payment just changed from coins to horses, flocks, herds and donkeys.

That's exactly what they say. They tell Joseph, "There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land." (Genesis 47:18) Money gone, livestock gone, and that's the list. I think that has to be a hard thing to say out loud.

Homes and tools are sensible things to count, but the Egyptians don't mention either one. They say, "There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land." (Genesis 47:18) Bodies and land. That's the whole list.

Tents and clothes never come up in this conversation. The Egyptians tell Joseph, "There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land." (Genesis 47:18) Their bodies and their land were the last two things on the list.

Yes. The Egyptians say, "Then we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:19) It's their own offer, made so they won't perish. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it there.
Soldiers would be a different deal entirely. The Egyptians don't offer to fight for anybody. They say, "we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:19) That's the word they use.

Builders sounds like a job, and this isn't described as one. What the Egyptians actually say is, "we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh." (Genesis 47:19) Their word is slaves, and that's the one the text keeps.

True. They ask, "Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not become desolate." (Genesis 47:19) Food gets them through today. Seed is what gets them a harvest later. They're asking for both.

It's true, friend, and the text is right there. They say, "Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not become desolate." (Genesis 47:19) They ask for food and for seed. Food for now, seed for the field.
The priests it is. The text says Joseph "did not acquire the priests' portion of the land." (Genesis 47:22) Everybody else's fields went to Pharaoh. The priests walked away still holding theirs.

Magicians do show up in Egypt in other places, so I see the guess. But in this passage they're not the group. Genesis 47:22 says Joseph "did not acquire the priests' portion of the land." Priests are the answer.

Guards would be a good guess if you're thinking about who works close to Pharaoh. But the text never mentions them here. It says Joseph "did not acquire the priests' portion of the land." (Genesis 47:22) That's the one group.

True, and the text gives the reason right away. The priests' land "had been given to them by Pharaoh. They ate the rations that Pharaoh supplied; so they did not sell their land." (Genesis 47:22) They had food coming in, so they had nothing to trade for it. No need to sell, so no sale.
It's true, friend. Genesis 47:22 says, "They ate the rations that Pharaoh supplied; so they did not sell their land." Pharaoh was already feeding them. That's the reason their land stayed theirs.

They keep it. Joseph says, "four-fifths will be yours as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children." (Genesis 47:24) One fifth to Pharaoh, four fifths for the people's own fields and tables. That's a lot of the batch staying in their kitchen.

The priests are in this passage, but not at this part of the deal. Joseph tells the people, "four-fifths will be yours as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children." (Genesis 47:24) The four-fifths stays with the people.

Joseph is handling the deal, but the four-fifths doesn't go to him. He says it will be "yours," meaning the people's, "as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children." (Genesis 47:24) The people keep it.

That's what they say. "You have saved our lives," they tell Joseph. "We have found favor in our lord's eyes, and we will be Pharaoh's servants." (Genesis 47:25) They have seed and food in front of them, and that's what they say first.

Nobody complains about the fifth. The people's answer is, "You have saved our lives… We have found favor in our lord's eyes, and we will be Pharaoh's servants." (Genesis 47:25) No objection about the share is recorded.

They already asked for seed earlier (Genesis 47:19), and Joseph has just handed it to them. When they hear his terms, they say, "You have saved our lives." (Genesis 47:25) No asking for more seed in this passage.

I get why you'd think that, since the famine is the whole reason for the deal. But the text says otherwise. Joseph established the law, "and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day." (Genesis 47:26) It doesn't stop when the famine does.

False, and the text says it plainly. "So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh, and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day." (Genesis 47:26) No end date is given. Only the priests' land is left out.
